texts.x: On 9 September, the Supreme Court dismissed a petition to reconsider its earlier verdict that lawyers fall outside the Consumer Protection Act. The rules are different for doctors.

points: On September 9, a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court dismissed a curative petition in Medico Legal Society of India v. Bar of Indian Lawyers & Ors.
The dismissal closed the final procedural resort to reconsider the 2024 ruling that lawyers do not fall within the Consumer Protection Act.
The author argues that an asymmetric legal gap exists where wronged patients can approach consumer forums, while wronged legal clients cannot.
In 1995, Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha held that a doctor treating a paying patient provides a service under consumer law.
Conversely, in Bar of Indian Lawyers v. D.K. Gandhi (2024), the court ruled that an advocate's work is a contract of personal service excluded from the Consumer Protection Act.
Arguments that lawyers owe duties to courts or cannot guarantee outcomes apply equally to doctors, who also follow strict medical ethics and professional codes.
The author notes that professions like architecture, chartered accountancy, and engineering occupy a similarly undefined space under consumer law.
With judicial avenues now closed, the author suggests that Parliament amend Section 2(42) to establish a clear, profession-neutral standard for specialised services.
sum.text:
I magine a situation wherein a doctor botches your treatment. You can drag them before a consumer forum and ask for compensation. The Right to Life and Personal Liberty guaranteed under Article 21 has been expanded by the Supreme Court to mean far more than just survival. It includes the right to live with dignity, an idea that extends into professional settings. This avenue is used often. Nearly 65,000 medical negligence cases were filed in 2025 alone, suggesting that the consumer forum is a genuine route for a remedy. Yet this same door does not exist for a client wronged by a lawyer, even when the harm is just as serious. This gap in law has just become a little more permanent now. points: Parliament passes a law and the President signs it, but the executive fails to issue a notification to commence it, leaving the statute dead on arrival.
This phenomenon, termed a notification veto, allows the government to indefinitely delay or refuse the implementation of statutes without judicial or legislative interference.
Prominent examples include the Delhi Rent Act of 1995 and the Whistleblowers Protection Act of 2014, which remain uncommenced decades after enactment.
Advocate Shobha Aggarwal filed a petition in 2025 challenging the non-commencement of the Delhi Rent Act after more than three decades of abeyance.
Supreme Court precedents like AK Roy (1981) and Aeltemesh Rein (1988) established that commencement discretion belongs to the executive but must be exercised fairly.
The government defends its inaction by arguing that commencement is a policy decision and that judicial intervention would violate the separation of powers.
The author suggests a workable fix where an inordinate delay places a burden on the government to justify itself or Parliament building automatic commencement clauses into statutes.

In one case, it's been more than 3 decades..Take the Delhi Rent Act. The President assented to it on August 23, 1995, but it has remained uncommenced ever since. This is because the decision on this lies with a Central government notification under Section 1(3), which has not been made in over three decades now.
Advocate Shobha Aggarwal took the matter to court in 2025..Parliament passed the Act. It was signed by the President; then it lay there, as nothing in the statute obliged the government to justify itself in any time frame. The Delhi Rent Act, 1995 is, therefore, now an Act that is on the statute book but not implemented to this day, waiting for a notification “on such date as the Central government may appoint.”.And this is not an isolated incident.
Another example of such a law is the National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995, which met the same fate and was finally done away with by Parliament through a new National Green Tribunal Act in 2010. There is also the Whistleblowers Protection Act of 2014, which became law on May 9, 2014 and has never been operational. According to a December 2025 parliamentary reply, the Act must be changed so that disclosures do not threaten India’s sovereignty and security.
The Amendment Bill, introduced in 2015, passed the Lok Sabha that year but could not reach the Rajya Sabha before the 16th Lok Sabha was dissolved in 2019..This pattern repeats across the 3 statutes: Parliament passes the Act the President signs the Act and the executive simply forgets to enforce the Act. What I refer to as a “notification veto” is not a legal theory, but merely a description of the constitutional impact of the failure to commence legislation..For more than 4 decades, the Supreme Court has grappled with this problem without answering its hardest version: when does commencement discretion stop being discretion and turn into indefinite refusal?.Look back on AK Roy v. Union of India, delivered in December 1981.
The Court declined to direct the government to notify a provision of the 44th Amendment, holding the discretion to be executive, not judicial. points: India's disability welfare system features parallel central and state programmes rather than integrated ones, leading to administrative silos.
The core goal is ensuring timely access to assistive technology and support services for persons with disabilities and senior citizens.
Central schemes like ADIP and RVY operate alongside state initiatives like Tamil Nadu's advanced assistive devices programme and Divyang Sahara Yojana.
Overlap is significant, with nine of the 15 major categories distributed by Tamil Nadu also provided under the central ADIP scheme.
Without shared beneficiary verification mechanisms, agencies cannot track coverage accurately, leading to potential gaps or duplicate provisioning.
Assistive technology is crucial for education and employment, meaning delayed access severely impacts the rights of persons with disabilities.
Fiscal constraints and matching fund requirements often hinder state participation in sharing implementation costs for welfare projects.
Solutions include bringing more states onto the ARJUN portal for unified data and utilizing flexible central sector funding models without mandatory matching.
Administrative convergence improves public spending efficiency, strengthens last-mile delivery, and powers India's emerging purple economy.

This ecosystem is built around a simple goal: enabling persons with disabilities (PwDs) and senior citizens to live with greater independence, dignity, and participation. Central to this is timely access to assistive technology and support services. Delivering these services requires a broad network of stakeholders. The Union government frames policy, provides funding, and supports implementation through specialised institutions. State governments deliver welfare through social welfare departments, district administrations, rehabilitation centres, and partnerships with civil society organisations. The analogy for the Cold War "red telephone" is obvious. But the comparison is apt only up to a point. The 1963 hotline worked because both sides understood what a nuclear incident looked like.
No such shared definition exists for an AI incident. What remains unclear is what kind of incidents would warrant using the channel, or what notifications each side would owe the other. A hotline without a threshold is a telephone that nobody knows when to pick up and talk.

In a rare gesture, the Supreme Court on Tuesday dedicated a judgment to a law clerk-cum-research associate who had assisted in a case on the detention of an accused under the National Security Act. In the same judgment, the court ruled that a confession made by an accused before a police officer cannot be the basis for detaining him under the NSA.
A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu expressed grief over the death of Ritwik Deswal, who worked in Justice Datta's office and died four days before his 27th birthday. The judges said the judgment carried the mark of his final work and recorded their appreciation for his research assistance.
"Human life is fragile. Yet, in the ordinary course of living, we seldom pause to recognise just how fleeting it is; and when life finally confronts us with that fragility, the realisation often comes too late. On that note, at the very outset, we begin on an unconventional premise," the bench said.
"One of our dearest law clerks-cum-research associates, Ritwik Deswal, left for his heavenly abode four days short of his 27th birthday, which happens to be today. As we pronounce this judgment, which bears the quiet and indelible imprint of his final labours, we wish to record our deep appreciation for the invaluable research assistance rendered by him in the build-up to the preparation of this judgment," it said.
The top court said Deswal's untimely death had left an "excruciatingly deep void". "Even in his final hours, his thoughts remained firmly anchored in the pursuit of truth and the service of justice. It is, therefore, with profound personal sorrow and grief that we dedicate this final collaboration to his memory, his integrity, his enduring commitment to the law, his love for academia, and his other great qualities of head and heart," the bench said.
On the legal issue, the apex court said preventive detention has always been regarded as an exceptional measure and must be used with the utmost circumspection. It said such power should be invoked only in the rarest of rare cases where the circumstances genuinely warrant it.

The act provides that if a birth or death is reported to the Registrar more than one year but within two years, it may be registered only with the approval of the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, or an Executive Magistrate.

In a statement, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways said that to promote ease of living for the citizens and further simplify toll-related procedures for Divyangjan and persons with disabilities (PwD), it has revised the guidelines for issuance and renewal of exempted FASTags for eligible Divyangjan/PwD beneficiaries.
